paragraphs: Image restoration must recover a useful image from damaged or incomplete visual information. Diffusion models can produce perceptually convincing results, but existing restoration systems often require expensive training for each task. DP-IR addresses this practical obstacle by connecting pretrained restoration networks with pretrained generative diffusion models through a small task-specific module.

The additional module has 0.7 million parameters. Its role is to let the framework combine the strengths of existing restoration and generation systems without requiring a newly trained diffusion model for every restoration task. The architecture also supports a sampling strategy that reduces neural function evaluations by at least fourfold without a reported performance loss. This strategy can be combined with acceleration methods such as DDIM.

The authors evaluate DP-IR on four benchmarks covering burst JDD-SR, dynamic scene deblurring, and super-resolution. They report better perceptual quality than existing approaches while remaining competitive on fidelity metrics. The distinction matters: the results support more convincing-looking reconstructions alongside competitive agreement with reference images, rather than claiming the best performance on every measure.
neurips-2024-a-modular-conditional-diffu.tldr: DP-IR combines pretrained restoration and diffusion models through a small task-specific module, improving perceptual quality while reducing sampling computation.

paragraphs: Testing whether a language model behaves consistently with human values requires scenarios that expose problematic responses. Expert-written benchmarks are expensive to expand, and fixed tests can struggle to keep pace with changing models or reveal rare risks. ALI-Agent uses language-model-powered agents to generate and adapt evaluation scenarios more automatically.

The framework separates this work into two stages. Emulation produces realistic situations for testing a target model. Refinement then iteratively modifies those situations to probe less common risks. A memory module guides scenario creation, a tool-using module reduces manual work such as evaluating model feedback, and an action module supports changes to the tests.

Experiments examine stereotypes, morality, and legality, with results showing that the framework identifies model misalignment across these areas. Additional analysis supports the meaningfulness of the generated use cases and the measures used to investigate long-tail risks. The contribution is an adaptive evaluation process that expands how misalignment can be investigated, with evidence grounded in these three tested aspects of human values.
neurips-2024-ali-agent-assessing-llms-al.tldr: ALI-Agent generates and iteratively refines realistic scenarios to uncover language-model misalignment involving stereotypes, morality, and legality.

paragraphs: In online optimization, regret measures how much cumulative loss an algorithm incurs relative to a comparator. Static regret uses one fixed comparator, while dynamic regret allows the comparator to change over time. This paper shows that, for linear losses, the dynamic problem can be expressed as a static problem in an enlarged decision space.

That connection provides a common framework for understanding tradeoffs between variation in the losses and movement of the comparator. The authors establish a frontier of lower bounds and describe how to achieve guarantees along it. They also prove that a proposed guarantee based on the squared movements of an arbitrary comparator sequence cannot generally be achieved.

The paper then replaces that unavailable guarantee with one based on a locally smoothed comparator sequence. Its algorithm controls dynamic regret using squared movements of the smoothed sequence, while retaining the usual worst-case dependence on path length up to polylogarithmic factors. This separates an impossible form of adaptation from a related achievable one and turns the equivalence into an algorithm-design tool.
neurips-2024-an-equivalence-between-stat.tldr: For linear losses, dynamic regret becomes static regret in a larger space, revealing achievable tradeoffs and an impossibility result for squared-path adaptation.

paragraphs: Neural operators can act on infinite-dimensional spaces, but their implementation requires finite-dimensional representations. This paper asks whether such representations can always approximate an operator continuously while preserving invertibility. Using category theory, it proves a negative result: some diffeomorphisms between Hilbert spaces do not admit the required continuous finite-dimensional approximations, even when nonlinear discretization is allowed.

The consequence concerns what discretization invariance demands. Convergence of the approximating functions alone is insufficient; their representations must also converge appropriately. This exposes a structural difference between infinite-dimensional Hilbert spaces and finite-dimensional vector spaces, rather than simply a difficulty caused by choosing an inadequate numerical resolution.

The authors also establish positive results under additional structure. Strongly monotone diffeomorphism operators admit finite-dimensional strongly monotone counterparts. Bilipschitz neural operators can be decomposed into alternating strongly monotone operators and invertible linear maps, and local iterative inversion is possible provided the inverse exists. The framework also yields quantitative discretization bounds. Together, these results identify both an obstruction to unrestricted discretization and useful structures for obtaining constructive guarantees.
neurips-2024-can-neural-operators-always.tldr: Continuous finite-dimensional discretization is not always possible for neural operators, but additional operator structure enables positive approximation results.

paragraphs: Recommendation models learn from historical user data that may contain sensitive information. Machine unlearning aims to remove selected data's influence from a trained model when that data should no longer be used. CURE4Rec addresses how to evaluate this process comprehensively, including consequences beyond whether a removal procedure appears to succeed.

The benchmark considers four dimensions: completeness of forgetting, usefulness of the remaining recommendations, computational efficiency of unlearning, and recommendation fairness. Measuring these together makes the evaluation broader than a test of forgetting alone. It also creates a shared framework for comparing methods whose removal procedures may affect recommendation behavior in different ways.

CURE4Rec evaluates removal requests involving core data, edge data, and randomly selected data. These strategies let the benchmark examine robustness to removing data with different levels of influence. The authors construct multiple datasets and extensively evaluate existing recommendation-unlearning methods. The stated contribution is the benchmark and its evaluation coverage, especially its attention to fairness and varying data impact; the abstract does not identify a single winning unlearning method.
neurips-2024-cure4rec-a-benchmark-for-re.tldr: CURE4Rec evaluates recommendation unlearning through forgetting completeness, recommendation utility, efficiency, and fairness across different data-removal strategies.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning builds a policy from an existing dataset. Diffusion-DICE starts from a distributional interpretation of DICE methods: their optimal stationary distribution ratio describes a transformation from the data-collection policy toward the optimized policy. The paper uses a diffusion model to carry out this transformation directly.

The key mathematical result splits the optimal policy's score function into a behavior-policy score and a guidance gradient determined by the optimal distribution ratio. A diffusion model trained on the dataset supplies the first component. The authors introduce an objective that learns the guidance component using only actions from the dataset, keeping this training step grounded in observed actions.

Because the resulting distribution can have multiple modes, guidance may lead to locally optimal choices. Diffusion-DICE therefore generates several candidate actions and selects among them to pursue the global optimum. The authors report that this guide-then-select approach minimizes exploitation of value-function errors. A toy example illustrates that failure mechanism in previous methods, and benchmark experiments demonstrate strong performance for Diffusion-DICE.
neurips-2024-diffusion-dice-in-sample-di.tldr: Diffusion-DICE learns diffusion guidance from dataset actions and selects among generated candidates to reduce exploitation of value-function errors in offline reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: Tabular prediction becomes harder when relationships in the data change over time. Drift-Resilient TabPFN learns a prediction procedure designed around this temporal drift. It takes the training dataset as context and predicts the test set in one forward pass, without requiring hyperparameter tuning for the new dataset.

Its training uses synthetic datasets generated from a prior built around structural causal models. A second causal model controls how the first model's parameters gradually change over time. By learning to approximate Bayesian inference under this prior, the network acquires an inductive bias toward the kinds of changing relationships represented during training.

Across 18 synthetic and real-world datasets, the authors report improvements over methods including XGB, CatBoost, TabPFN, and applicable Wild-Time methods. Against the strongest baselines, reported accuracy increases from 0.688 to 0.744 and ROC AUC from 0.786 to 0.832, alongside stronger calibration. The method runs in seconds on small to moderately sized datasets. These findings support learning temporal adaptation through the training prior in the evaluated settings.
neurips-2024-drift-resilient-tabpfn-in-c.tldr: Drift-Resilient TabPFN learns from synthetic causal models that change over time, improving tabular prediction under temporal distribution shifts.

paragraphs: Physics-informed neural networks solve differential equations by minimizing losses for both the equation residual and its boundary conditions. These objectives can produce problematic training signals. The paper identifies a harmful situation in which their gradients differ greatly in magnitude and have a negative inner product, meaning their directions conflict.

Dual Cone Gradient Descent adjusts the gradient used for an update so that it lies in a region having nonnegative inner products with both component gradients. This geometric constraint addresses how the two objectives interact, rather than relying only on the combined loss value. The authors also analyze the convergence properties of the resulting algorithms in a nonconvex setting.

Across benchmark equations, DCGD improves evaluation metrics relative to other optimizers. The reported benefits include greater predictive accuracy and more stable training on difficult equations and known PINN failure cases, compared with optimally tuned existing models. It can also be combined with learning-rate annealing and Neural Tangent Kernel strategies for further improvement. The findings connect a specific gradient conflict to a practical optimization intervention.
neurips-2024-dual-cone-gradient-descent-.tldr: DCGD adjusts conflicting physics and boundary-loss gradients, improving the accuracy and training stability of physics-informed neural networks on benchmark equations.

paragraphs: Diffusion policies can represent complicated action distributions, making them useful for offline reinforcement learning. However, a fixed dataset leaves uncertainty about unfamiliar actions, and learned Q-functions can assign those actions overly optimistic values. This paper combines an entropy-regularized diffusion policy with an ensemble of Q-functions to address that problem.

The policy uses a mean-reverting stochastic differential equation to transform the action distribution into a standard Gaussian. A corresponding reverse-time process generates actions conditioned on the environment state. The authors show that this policy has tractable entropy, allowing entropy regularization to encourage exploration of out-of-distribution samples during offline training.

The Q-ensemble supplies a complementary safeguard: action values are estimated pessimistically using a lower confidence bound. The design therefore combines broader action sampling with caution about uncertain value predictions. Across a range of D4RL tasks, the authors report state-of-the-art performance and substantial improvements over existing diffusion policies. These results support the combined policy-and-value design in the evaluated offline reinforcement-learning settings.
neurips-2024-entropy-regularized-diffusi.tldr: An entropy-regularized diffusion policy paired with pessimistic Q-ensemble estimates improves offline reinforcement-learning performance on D4RL tasks.

paragraphs: A few demonstrations may show what an agent does without explicitly stating its goal or motion style. FTL-IGM treats learning that underlying intent as task concept learning. It first trains an invertible generative model on basic concepts and demonstrations, establishing a reusable relationship between task concepts and the behavior they produce.

For a new concept, the method works backward from a small set of demonstrations. Backpropagation adjusts the inferred concept while leaving the pretrained model's weights unchanged. The model's invertibility enables this inference procedure. Once a concept has been learned, the generative model can use it to produce corresponding plans or motions.

The authors evaluate the approach in five domains: object rearrangement, goal-oriented navigation, human-action motion caption, autonomous driving, and real-world tabletop manipulation. Their experiments show successful learning of novel concepts and generation in unseen environments or in combination with training concepts. The central finding is that a pretrained generative model can support both inferring intent from sparse examples and reusing that intent to generate behavior in these tested settings.
neurips-2024-few-shot-task-learning-thro.tldr: FTL-IGM infers new task concepts from a few demonstrations through a fixed invertible generative model, then generates corresponding plans or motions.

paragraphs: Multimodal prediction combines information from sources such as images, text, and personal records. In practice, different examples may contain different subsets of those sources. Flex-MoE addresses this variation with a mixture-of-experts framework designed to handle arbitrary modality combinations, including cases where some inputs are missing.

The framework first uses a missing-modality bank to connect the observed combination with its missing modalities. It then applies a sparse mixture of experts with two routing roles. A generalized router trains experts on complete examples to establish shared knowledge. A specialized router handles reduced modality combinations by assigning the top-ranked gate to the expert associated with the observed combination.

This design makes input availability part of the routing decision, while retaining knowledge learned from complete data. The authors evaluate it on ADNI, with four modalities in the Alzheimer's disease domain, and on MIMIC-IV. Their results demonstrate effectiveness across diverse missing-modality scenarios. The evidence supports combining general expert knowledge with combination-specific routing for prediction when the available sources vary between examples.
neurips-2024-flex-moe-modeling-arbitrary.tldr: Flex-MoE combines a missing-modality bank with general and specialized expert routing to handle varying combinations of available inputs.

paragraphs: An image can be divided meaningfully at several levels: small parts, whole objects, or larger scene regions. This makes unsupervised semantic segmentation ambiguous because there may be no single appropriate level of detail. The paper addresses that ambiguity by discovering nested regions instead of relying on dataset-specific choices about semantic granularity.

The method uses representations learned by self-supervised models to guide an algebraic procedure that recursively splits an image into subgraphs. It estimates how many subgraphs are needed and separates them clearly. The resulting tree organizes scene-specific primitives and semantic regions, capturing both fine and coarse structure without predefined region categories.

The authors also introduce a metric for evaluating discovered elements at different hierarchy levels and assessing compositional relationships among parts, objects, and scenes. Experiments across datasets report better semantic hierarchical relationships and segmentation than existing unsupervised approaches. The contribution is therefore both a way to construct multilevel image structure and a way to evaluate whether the discovered hierarchy reflects meaningful relationships between scene elements.
neurips-2024-hierarchy-agnostic-unsuperv.tldr: A recursive graph-based method discovers nested semantic image regions without predefined categories and evaluates their relationships across hierarchy levels.

paragraphs: Membership inference asks whether a particular example was included in a model's training data. For large vision-language models, this question can involve sensitive images as well as text. The paper addresses a gap in evaluation infrastructure and methods for investigating training-data membership in models that process both modalities.

The authors introduce a benchmark tailored to multiple vision-language models, providing a common setting for studying these attacks. They also develop a pipeline for image membership detection at the token level. This specifically extends the investigation to image information as represented within the model, rather than treating membership detection solely as a text problem.

A further contribution is MaxRényi-K%, a metric based on confidence in model outputs that applies to both text and images. Together, the benchmark, image-detection pipeline, and confidence-based metric provide tools for investigating potentially inappropriate training-data use. The abstract presents these methodological contributions without reporting a numerical detection result, so their stated significance lies in enabling more systematic membership-inference research for vision-language models.
neurips-2024-membership-inference-attack.tldr: The paper introduces a vision-language membership-inference benchmark, a token-level image-detection pipeline, and a confidence-based metric usable for text and images.

paragraphs: Knowing that a quantum circuit can approximate a function eventually does not establish what it can achieve with limited resources. This paper studies parameterized quantum circuits through explicit constructions and finite-resource error bounds. It focuses on multivariate polynomials and smooth functions, connecting approximation quality to concrete circuit requirements.

The authors construct data re-uploading circuits and bound their error in terms of qubit count, circuit depth, and number of trainable parameters. This addresses weaknesses in earlier universal approximation results that were either nonconstructive or relied on trainable classical processing. Explicit quantum constructions help clarify which approximation capability is attributable to the quantum circuit itself.

For the function classes studied, the authors show that their circuits can require smaller circuit size and fewer trainable parameters than deep ReLU networks. They also demonstrate approximation capability numerically. This is a qualified resource comparison for the proposed constructions, rather than a universal advantage for quantum machine learning. The bounds provide a basis for designing circuits around the limited resources available on near-term quantum devices.
neurips-2024-non-asymptotic-approximatio.tldr: Explicit quantum-circuit constructions yield finite-resource approximation bounds and can use fewer resources than deep ReLU networks for the studied function classes.

paragraphs: Feature learning involves choosing how to represent data as well as how to predict from that representation. This paper studies a simplified version: empirical risk minimization jointly chooses a feature map from a collection and a linear predictor, using squared regression loss. The question is how much that choice costs statistically.

The authors compare this learner with an oracle that already knows the best feature map and only fits the corresponding linear model. When the collection is not too large and the optimal feature map is unique, asymptotic quantiles of excess risk agree with the oracle's up to a factor of two. Thus, under these conditions, learning the representation can approach the performance of knowing it beforehand.

A complementary finite-sample analysis quantifies how the influence of the collection's overall complexity decays. It relates that influence to the size of sets containing nearly optimal feature maps. The authors apply the results to best subset selection in sparse linear regression, characterizing its performance under general assumptions. The contribution connects representation selection with both oracle comparisons and finite-sample statistical guarantees.
neurips-2024-on-the-efficiency-of-erm-in.tldr: Under stated conditions, empirical risk minimization that learns a feature map approaches the excess-risk behavior of an oracle that already knows the best map.

paragraphs: Scientific prediction often needs to combine measured data with differential equations describing the underlying system. Gaussian processes are useful here because they can incorporate prior knowledge, represent nonlinear behavior, and quantify uncertainty. Existing physics-informed GP methods, however, can be computationally expensive or restricted to processes that vary only over time.

This paper introduces a variational state-space Gaussian process for phenomena that vary across both space and time. The model accommodates linear and nonlinear physical constraints while achieving computational cost that grows linearly with the temporal extent of the problem. That scaling addresses the time-related computational burden while preserving a setting that includes spatial variation.

The authors test the approach on synthetic and real-world problems and report improvements over the current state of the art in both predictive and computational performance. These findings support the proposed combination of physical constraints, uncertainty-aware modeling, and efficient temporal computation. The contribution is particularly about bringing these capabilities into one spatiotemporal framework, rather than obtaining efficiency by restricting the model to time alone.
neurips-2024-physics-informed-variationa.tldr: A variational state-space Gaussian process incorporates linear and nonlinear physics across space and time with computational cost linear in time.

paragraphs: Neural radiance fields reconstruct scenes from images, but reconstruction quality depends partly on the viewpoints that observe each scene point. The arrangement of those viewpoints affects triangulation quality. ProvNeRF explicitly models this information, addressing the absence of a representation for training-camera pose distributions in existing work identified by the authors.

For each point, provenance means the locations from which that point is likely visible. ProvNeRF represents this provenance as a stochastic field, allowing it to describe a distribution rather than a single viewing location. To learn that field, the authors extend implicit maximum likelihood estimation into functional space and provide an objective that can be optimized alongside the NeRF.

Learning provenance gives the reconstruction information about its triangulation support. In the challenging setting of sparse, unconstrained views, the authors report improvements in both novel-view synthesis and uncertainty estimation against competitive baselines. The result links the quality of the available camera evidence to the learned scene representation, with empirical benefits for rendering new viewpoints and estimating uncertainty.
neurips-2024-provnerf-modeling-per-point.tldr: ProvNeRF learns where each scene point is likely visible, improving novel-view synthesis and uncertainty estimation with sparse, unconstrained camera views.

paragraphs: A Gaussian mixture represents a distribution as several Gaussian components. This paper asks how many samples suffice to learn such a mixture accurately while satisfying approximate differential privacy. Accuracy is measured in total variation distance, so the goal concerns recovering the overall distribution with low error.

For k arbitrary Gaussian components in d dimensions, the authors prove a sufficient sample count of roughly kd² + k^1.5 d^1.75 + k²d. This improves the previous bound of roughly k²d⁴. They also establish that the new result is optimal in the regime where d is much larger than k², making the optimality claim conditional on that relationship between dimension and component count.

The paper separately gives an optimal result for mixtures of one-dimensional Gaussians, reducing dependence on the number of components from quadratic to linear. Its algorithms combine inverse sensitivity, distribution sample compression, and bounds on volumes of sumsets. These contributions improve the amount of data needed for private distribution learning and identify regimes where that requirement is provably optimal.
neurips-2024-sample-efficient-private-le.tldr: The paper improves sample bounds for privately learning Gaussian mixtures, with optimal results in a high-dimensional regime and for one-dimensional mixtures.

paragraphs: Subsampling makes large rare-event datasets cheaper to analyze, but discarding observations can reduce statistical efficiency. Existing optimal sampling rules can also change when features are rescaled. This is especially problematic for sparse models: rescaling an inactive feature can give it arbitrarily large influence over which observations are selected.

The paper develops a scale-invariant sampling rule by optimizing prediction error instead of focusing on parameter estimation. Using adaptive lasso, the authors first establish oracle properties for rare-event estimation. They then derive sampling probabilities that minimize prediction error for an inverse-probability-weighted adaptive lasso estimator, tying the sampling objective directly to predictive performance.

A further estimator based on maximum sampled conditional likelihood is introduced to improve estimation efficiency. Experiments on simulated and real-world datasets demonstrate the proposed methods' performance. The central contribution is to make optimal subsampling insensitive to feature scaling in the sparse-model setting, so irrelevant features cannot gain sampling influence merely through their units or numerical scale. The theoretical analysis and estimator design support that objective together.
neurips-2024-scale-invariant-optimal-sam.tldr: A prediction-focused subsampling rule remains invariant to feature scaling, improving the design of rare-event estimation for sparse models.

paragraphs: Complex image generation requires coordinating multiple objects, their attributes, and their relationships. This paper uses scene graphs to make that structure explicit, then separates the graph's visual guidance into components that can be recombined. The aim is to generate coherent scenes while providing control over their content.

A Semantics-Layout Variational AutoEncoder jointly derives semantic information and spatial layouts from the graph. Its one-to-many mapping allows a single graph to support diverse plausible visual arrangements. A diffusion model then uses Compositional Masked Attention to incorporate those layouts, semantics, and fine-grained attributes as generation guidance.

For editing, a Multi-Layered Sampler supports graph changes while keeping other visual content consistent, producing an isolated editing effect. Experiments report improvements over recent text-, layout-, and scene-graph-based competitors in generation rationality and controllability. The contribution links structured scene descriptions to both diverse generation and targeted modification: objects and relationships guide the image without forcing every graph to correspond to only one visual realization.
neurips-2024-scene-graph-disentanglement.tldr: The method turns scene graphs into separate semantic and layout cues for controllable diffusion generation and localized, visually consistent editing.

paragraphs: An adversarial example changes an input enough to make a neural network predict incorrectly. When evaluating robustness, a useful question is how small that change can be. This paper focuses on minimal perturbations measured by the ℓ2 norm, for which existing evaluation methods can be expensive or insufficiently accurate.

The authors introduce a family of attacks that generalizes DeepFool while remaining simple to understand and implement. Their goal is to balance the effectiveness of finding small adversarial changes with the computational cost of doing so. This matters because the quality and expense of the attack affect how practically a model's robustness can be evaluated.

The reported experiments show improvements over existing methods in both effectiveness and computational efficiency. The attacks are also presented as suitable for large-model evaluation and for adversarial training, where generated attacks become part of the training process. In that training role, the authors report state-of-the-art robustness to minimal ℓ2 perturbations. The claimed benefits concern this specific robustness measure and the evaluated attack and training settings.
neurips-2024-superdeepfool-a-new-fast-an.tldr: SuperDeepFool generalizes DeepFool to find small ℓ2 adversarial perturbations more effectively and efficiently, supporting robustness evaluation and adversarial training.

paragraphs: Inferring a person's three-dimensional pose from a single image is uncertain, especially when body parts are hidden. Diffusion models can represent that uncertainty, but their large search spaces and training-data demands can lead to biomechanically unrealistic results. Di²Pose addresses this issue by modeling poses in a discrete representation.

The method has two stages. First, pose quantization converts three-dimensional poses into discrete representations. A discrete diffusion process then models those representations in latent space. This confines the search toward physically viable configurations and helps the model capture how occlusion affects pose information within that representation.

The authors evaluate the framework on multiple benchmarks, including Human3.6M, 3DPW, and 3DPW-Occ, and report evidence of its effectiveness. The central contribution is the representation used for diffusion: the model reasons over quantized pose configurations to narrow a difficult reconstruction problem. That structure is intended to reduce implausible possibilities while retaining diffusion's ability to address uncertainty, particularly when the image does not reveal the full body.
neurips-2024-text-di-2-text-pose-discret.tldr: Di²Pose uses pose quantization and discrete diffusion to narrow the search toward plausible three-dimensional human poses under occlusion.

paragraphs: A vision-language model such as CLIP can struggle when downstream images differ substantially from its pretraining data. Meanwhile, other pretrained models contain useful expertise from different modalities, tasks, architectures, and datasets. TransAgent aims to bring that distributed knowledge into a single vision-language model despite the experts' heterogeneous structures.

The framework uses a unified knowledge-transfer process and multi-source distillation to guide CLIP. In the reported setup, it collaborates with 11 heterogeneous expert agents. Their knowledge strengthens the target model without adding inference-time cost, so the resulting predictions do not require an additional computational burden from the participating experts.

Across 11 visual recognition datasets, the authors report state-of-the-art performance. Under the same low-shot conditions, TransAgent outperforms CoOp by around 10% on average and 20% on EuroSAT, which has large domain shifts. These results support using diverse pretrained expertise to improve transfer when labeled target examples are scarce. The contribution is both a way to unify otherwise separate models' knowledge and evidence that this transfer improves downstream recognition.
neurips-2024-transagent-transfer-vision-.tldr: TransAgent distills knowledge from 11 heterogeneous experts into a vision-language model, improving low-shot recognition without additional inference cost.

paragraphs: In-context learning lets a Transformer use demonstrations without updating its parameters. One proposed explanation is that its layers internally perform gradient descent. This paper examines linear regression and finds behavior closer to a second-order optimization procedure, Iterative Newton's Method, which converges exponentially faster than gradient descent in the studied comparison.

Empirically, predictions at successive Transformer layers closely track different Newton iterations through a linear relationship. Each middle layer roughly corresponds to three iterations, yielding a similar convergence rate. The authors also show learning on ill-conditioned data, where gradient descent struggles but Iterative Newton's Method succeeds.

To support the empirical evidence, the paper proves that a Transformer can implement k Newton iterations using k plus a constant number of layers. This establishes an architectural capability alongside observations of learned behavior. The result offers a more powerful account of in-context computation for linear regression: Transformers can approximate second-order methods, with both layerwise evidence and a constructive theoretical explanation supporting that claim in this setting.
neurips-2024-transformers-learn-to-achie.tldr: For in-context linear regression, Transformers exhibit Newton-like convergence, and a construction shows they can implement Newton iterations with nearly one layer per iteration.

paragraphs: Self-supervised graph learning pretrains graph neural networks without labels, but successful pretraining does not mean every learned parameter is useful. This paper investigates redundancy at both the neuron and layer levels. Its experiments show substantial redundancy: randomly removing 51.6% of parameters still retains at least 96.2% of performance in the reported finding.

The authors use this observation to motivate SLIDE, a graph pretraining and fine-tuning approach named SLImming DE-correlation Fine-tuning. Reducing the pretrained model makes joint fine-tuning of the graph network and prediction layers more feasible. The approach therefore treats model reduction as part of downstream adaptation, rather than assuming the entire pretrained network must be retained.

Across benchmarks, SLIDE is effective and often improves performance with fewer parameters. For GraphMAE on Amazon-Computers, randomly removing 40% of parameters produces reported Micro-F1 and Macro-F1 improvements of 0.24% and 0.27% over full fine-tuning. These empirical results show that substantial parameter removal can preserve or improve downstream performance in the tested settings, challenging the assumption that all pretrained capacity contributes equally.
neurips-2024-uncovering-the-redundancy-i.tldr: Graph self-supervised models show substantial parameter redundancy, motivating SLIDE's smaller models that often improve downstream fine-tuning performance.
